entries.ca87479256aa294399c15c4dafdf8a23c7bb7937: <div sID="gen3320" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="34" osisID="Num.34" sID="Num.34"/> <div eID="gen3320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3321" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3322" type="x-p"/> In this chapter God directs Moses, and he is to direct Israel, I. Concerning the bounds and borders of the land of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Num.34.1-Num.34.15">ver. 1-15</reference>. II. Concerning the division and distribution of it to the tribes of Israel, <reference osisRef="Num.34.16-Num.34.29">ver. 16</reference>, &c.
entries.56107c8726827b0252cb2e7ffbb96dfbf89b0030: <div eID="gen3322" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Boundaries of Canaan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3323" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Command the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye come into the land of Canaan; (this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the land that shall fall unto you for an inheritance, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the land of Canaan with the coasts thereof:) <hi type="super">3</hi> Then your south quarter shall be from the wilderness of Zin along by the coast of Edom, and your south border shall be the outmost coast of the salt sea eastward: <hi type="super">4</hi> And your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim, and pass on to Zin: and the going forth thereof shall be from the south to Kadesh-barnea, and shall go on to Hazar-addar, and pass on to Azmon: <hi type="super">5</hi> And the border shall fetch a compass from Azmon unto the river of Egypt, and the goings out of it shall be at the sea. <hi type="super">6</hi> And <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the western border, ye shall even have the great sea for a border: this shall be your west border. <hi type="super">7</hi> And this shall be your north border: from the great sea ye shall point out for you mount Hor: <hi type="super">8</hi> From mount Hor ye shall point out <hi type="italic">your border</hi> unto the entrance of Hamath; and the goings forth of the border shall be to Zedad: <hi type="super">9</hi> And the border shall go on to Ziphron, and the goings out of it shall be at Hazar-enan: this shall be your north border. <hi type="super">10</hi> And ye shall point out your east border from Hazar-enan to Shepham: <hi type="super">11</hi> And the coast shall go down from Shepham to Riblah, on the east side of Ain; and the border shall descend, and shall reach unto the side of the sea of Chinnereth eastward: <hi type="super">12</hi> And the border shall go down to Jordan, and the goings out of it shall be at the salt sea: this shall be your land with the coasts thereof round about. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Moses commanded the children of Israel, saying, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the land which ye shall inherit by lot, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded to give unto the nine tribes, and to the half tribe: <hi type="super">14</hi> For the tribe of the children of Reuben according to the house of their fathers, and the tribe of the children of Gad according to the house of their fathers, have received <hi type="italic">their inheritance;</hi> and half the tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance: <hi type="super">15</hi> The two tribes and the half tribe have received their inheritance on this side Jordan <hi type="italic">near</hi> Jericho eastward, toward the sunrising. <div eID="gen3323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3324" type="x-p"/> We have here a particular draught of the line by which the land of Canaan was meted, and bounded, on all sides. God directs Moses to settle it here, not as a geographer in his map, merely to please the curious, but as a prince in his grant, that it may be certainly known what passes, and is conveyed, by the grant. There was a much larger possession promised them, which in due time they would have possessed if they had been obedient, reaching even to the river Euphrates, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.24">Deut. xi. 24</reference>. And even so far the dominion of Israel did extend in David's time and Solomon's, <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.26">2 Chron. ix. 26</reference>. But this which is here described is Canaan only, which was the lot of the nine tribes and a half, for the other two and a half were already settled, <reference osisRef="Num.34.14-Num.34.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. Now concerning the limits of Canaan observe, <div eID="gen3324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3325" type="x-p"/> I. That it was limited within certain bounds: for God <hi type="italic">appoints the bounds of our habitation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Acts xvii. 26</reference>. The borders are set them, 1. That they might know whom they were to dispossess, and how far the commission which was given them extended (<reference osisRef="Num.33.53">ch. xxxiii. 53</reference>), that they should <hi type="italic">drive out the inhabitants.</hi> Those that lay within these borders, and those only, they must destroy; hitherto their bloody sword must go, and no further. 2. That they might know what to expect the possession of themselves. God would not have his people to enlarge their desire of worldly possessions, but to know when they have enough, and to rest satisfied with it. The Israelites themselves must not be <hi type="italic">placed alone in the midst of the earth,</hi> but must leave room for their neighbours to live by them. God sets bounds to our lot; let us then set bounds to our desires, and bring our mind to our condition. <div eID="gen3325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3326" type="x-p"/> II. That it lay comparatively in a very little compass: as it is here bounded, it is reckoned to be but about 160 miles in length and about fifty in breadth; perhaps it did not contain more than half as much ground as England, and yet this is the country which was promised to the father of the faithful and was the possession of the seed of Israel. This was that little spot of ground in which only, for many ages, <hi type="italic">God was known, and his name was great,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1">Ps. lxxvi. 1</reference>. This was the vineyard of the Lord, the garden enclosed; but, as it is with gardens and vineyards, the narrowness of the extent was abundantly compensated by the extraordinary fruitfulness of the soil, otherwise it could not have subsisted so numerous a nation as did inhabit it. See here then, 1. How small a part of the world God has for himself. Though the <hi type="italic">earth is his, and the fullness thereof,</hi> yet few have the knowledge of him and serve him; but those few are happy, very happy, because fruitful to God. 2. How small a share of the world God often gives to his own people. Those that have their portion in heaven have reason to be content with a small pittance of this earth; but, as here, what is wanting in quantity is made up in quality; <hi type="italic">a little that a righteous man has,</hi> having it from the love of God and with his blessing, is far better and more comfortable <hi type="italic">than the riches of many wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">Ps. xxxvii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen3326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3327" type="x-p"/> III. It is observable what the bounds and limits of it were. 1. Canaan was itself a <hi type="italic">pleasant land</hi> (so it is called <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Dan. viii. 9</reference>), and yet it bordered upon wilderness and seas, and was surrounded with divers melancholy prospects. Thus the vineyard of the church is compassed on all hands with the desert of this world, which serves as a foil to it, to make it appear the more beautiful for situation. 2. Many of its borders were its defences and natural fortifications, to render the access of enemies the more difficult, and to intimate to Israel that the God of nature was their protector, and with his favour would <hi type="italic">compass them as with a shield.</hi> 3. The border reached to the <hi type="italic">river of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.34.5">v. 5</reference>), that the sight of that country which they could look into out of their own might remind them of their bondage there, and their wonderful deliverance thence. 4. Their border is here made to begin at the <hi type="italic">Salt Sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.34.3">v. 3</reference>), and there it ends, <reference osisRef="Num.34.12">v. 12</reference>. This was the remaining lasting monument of the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. That pleasant fruitful vale in which these cities stood became a lake, which was never stirred by any wind, bore no vessels, was replenished with no fish, no living creature of any sort being found in it, therefore called the <hi type="italic">Dead Sea.</hi> This was part of their border, that it might be a constant warning to them to take heed of those sins which had been the ruin of Sodom; yet the iniquity of Sodom was afterwards found in Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.49">Ezek. xvi. 49</reference>), for which Canaan was made, though not a salt sea as Sodom, yet a barren soil, and continues so to this day. 5. Their western border was the <hi type="italic">Great Sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.34.6">v. 6</reference>), which is now called the <hi type="italic">Mediterranean.</hi> Some consider this sea itself to have been a part of their possession, and that by virtue of this grant, they had the dominion of it, and, if they had not forfeited it by sin, might have rode masters of it.
entries.e9fd6322167aaa606d875f4792ab16d482b1ace9: <div eID="gen3327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3328" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">17</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the names of the men which shall divide the land unto you: Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun. <hi type="super">18</hi> And ye shall take one prince of every tribe, to divide the land by inheritance. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the names of the men <hi type="italic">are</hi> these: Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh. <hi type="super">20</hi> And of the tribe of the children of Simeon, Shemuel the son of Ammihud. <hi type="super">21</hi> Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the prince of the tribe of the children of Dan, Bukki the son of Jogli. <hi type="super">23</hi> The prince of the children of Joseph, for the tribe of the children of Manasseh, Hanniel the son of Ephod. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the prince of the tribe of the children of Ephraim, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan. 25 And the prince of the tribe of the children of Zebulun, Elizaphan the son of Parnach. <hi type="super">26</hi> And the prince of the tribe of the children of Issachar, Paltiel the son of Azzan. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the prince of the tribe of the children of Asher, Ahihud the son of Shelomi. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the prince of the tribe of the children of Naphtali, Pedahel the son of Ammihud. <hi type="super">29</hi> These <hi type="italic">are they</hi> whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded to divide the inheritance unto the children of Israel in the land of Canaan. <div eID="gen3328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3329" type="x-p"/> God here appoints commissioners for the dividing of the land to them. The conquest of it is taken for granted, though as yet there was never a stroke struck towards it. Here is no nomination of the generals and commanders-in-chief that should carry on the war; for they were to get the land in possession, <hi type="italic">not by their own sword or bow, but by the power and favour of God;</hi> and so confident must they be of victory and success while God fought for them that the persons must now be named who should be entrusted with the dividing of the land, that is, who should preside in casting the lots, and determine controversies that might arise, and see that all was done fairly. 1. The principal commissioners, who were of the <hi type="italic">quorum,</hi> were Eleazar and Joshua (<reference osisRef="Num.34.17">v. 17</reference>), typifying Christ, who, as priest and king, divides the heavenly Canaan to the spiritual Israel; yet, as they were to go by the lot, so Christ acknowledges the disposal must be by the will of the Father, <reference osisRef="Matt.20.23">Matt. xx. 23</reference>. Compare, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Eph. i. 11</reference>. 2. Besides these, that there might be no suspicion of partiality, a prince of each tribe was appointed to inspect this matter, and to see that the tribe he served for was in no respect injured. Public affairs should be so managed as not only to give their right to all, but, if possible, to give satisfaction to all that they have justice done them., It is a happiness to a land to have the princes of their people meet together, some out of every tribe, to concert the affairs that are of common concern, a constitution which is the abundant honour, ease, and safety, of the nation that is blessed with it. 3. Some observe that the order of the tribes here very much differs from that in which they hitherto, upon all occasions, been named, and agrees with the neighbourhood of their lots in the division of the land. Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, the first three here named, lay close together; the inheritance of Dan lay next them on one side, that of Ephraim and Manasseh on another side; Zebulun and Issachar lay abreast more northerly, and, lastly, Asher and Naphtali most northward of all, as is easy to observe in looking over a map of Canaan; this (says bishop Patrick) is an evidence that Moses was guided by a divine Spirit in his writings. Known unto God are all his works beforehand, and what is new and surprising to us he perfectly foresaw, without any confusion or uncertainty.  <chapter eID="Num.34"/> <div eID="gen3329" type="x-p"/>

entries.51f63b3fb3e168d89d8ad7222b7b25541c241119: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1623"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 34</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.34.1-Num.34.29">Nu 34:1-29</reference>. The Borders of the Land of Canaan.</title> <div sID="gen2174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1623"/><hi type="bold">2. this is the ... land of Canaan--</hi>The details given in this chapter mark the general boundary of the inheritance of Israel west of the Jordan. The Israelites never actually possessed all the territory comprised within these boundaries, even when it was most extended by the conquests of David and Solomon. <div eID="gen2174" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fb80d8c298e13a5b5b56cb3806b36e3e1e4e495: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1624"/><div sID="gen2175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1624"/><hi type="bold">3-5. your south quarter--</hi>The line which bounded it on the south is the most difficult to trace. According to the best biblical geographers, the leading points here defined are as follows: The southwest angle of the southern boundary should be where the wilderness of Zin touches the border of Edom, so that the southern boundary should extend eastward from the extremity of the Dead Sea, wind around the precipitous ridge of Akrabbim ("scorpions"), thought to be the high and difficult Pass of Safeh, which crosses the stream that flows from the south into the Jordan--that is, the great valley of the Arabah, reaching from the Dead to the Red Sea. <div eID="gen2175" type="x-p"/>
entries.56357262c5346b992d2088e07f7c6a471e4e8e06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1626"/><div sID="gen2177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1626"/><hi type="bold">6. the western border--</hi>There is no uncertainty about this boundary, as it is universally allowed to be the Mediterranean, which is called "the great sea" in comparison with the small inland seas or lakes known to the Hebrews. <div eID="gen2177" type="x-p"/>
entries.aee8231d75b68c3034b25795f7e1a8884e5df242: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1627"/><div sID="gen2178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1627"/><hi type="bold">7-9. north border--</hi>The principal difficulty in understanding the description here arises from what our translators have called mount Hor. The Hebrew words, however, Hor-ha-Hor, properly signify "the mountain of the mountain," or "the high double mountain," which, from the situation, can mean nothing else than the mountain Amana (<reference osisRef="Song.4.8">So 4:8</reference>), a member of the great Lebanon range (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.5">Jos 13:5</reference>). <div eID="gen2178" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fe99438094ea83a152bc1e6292a8d22b71620ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1630"/><div sID="gen2183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1630"/><hi type="bold">10-12. east border--</hi>This is very clearly defined. Shepham and Riblah, which were in the valley of Lebanon, are mentioned as the boundary line, which commenced a little higher than the sources of the Jordan. Ain is supposed to be the source of that river; and thence the eastern boundary extended along the Jordan, the sea of Chinnereth (Lake of Tiberias), the Jordan; and again terminated at the Dead Sea. The line being drawn on the east of the river and the seas included those waters within the territory of the western tribes. <div eID="gen2183" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bef1bff188441995d42ae25be4405789a86b9e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1631"/><div sID="gen2184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1631"/><hi type="bold">13-15. The two tribes and the half-tribe have received their inheritance on this side Jordan--</hi>The conquered territories of Sihon and Og, lying between the Arnon and mount Hermon, were allotted to them--that of Reuben in the most southerly part, Gad north of it, and the half Manasseh in the northernmost portion. <div eID="gen2184" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e5c30f4d7df67f366f7529327575d361705f716: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1632"/><div sID="gen2185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1632"/><hi type="bold">16-29. names of the men ... which shall divide the land--</hi>This appointment by the Lord before the Jordan tended not only to animate the Israelites faith in the certainty of the conquest, but to prevent all subsequent dispute and discontent, which might have been dangerous in presence of the natives. The nominees were ten princes for the nine and a half tribes, one of them being selected from the western section of Manasseh, and all subordinate to the great military and ecclesiastical chiefs, Joshua and Eleazar. The names are mentioned in the exact order in which the tribes obtained possession of the land, and according to brotherly connection. <chapter eID="Num.34"/>

entries.93849d3574b76a6bc86c1049d748e7012073d698: <div eID="gen6283" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6284" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6285" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6285" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6284" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6286" type="x-p"/> The land of Canaan is described, <reference osisRef="Num.34.1">Num 34:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.34.2">Num 34:2</reference>. The south quarter, <reference osisRef="Num.34.3-Num.34.5">Num 34:3-5</reference>. The western border, <reference osisRef="Num.34.6">Num 34:6</reference>. The north border, <reference osisRef="Num.34.7-Num.34.9">Num 34:7-9</reference>. The east border, <reference osisRef="Num.34.10-Num.34.12">Num 34:10-12</reference>. This land to be divided by lot among the nine tribes and half, <reference osisRef="Num.34.13">Num 34:13</reference>; two tribes and half, Reuben and Gad, and the half of Manasseh, having already got their inheritance on the east side of Jordan, <reference osisRef="Num.34.14">Num 34:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.34.15">Num 34:15</reference>. Eleazar the priest, and Joshua, to assist in dividing the land, <reference osisRef="Num.34.16">Num 34:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.34.17">Num 34:17</reference>; and with them a chief out of every tribe, <reference osisRef="Num.34.18">Num 34:18</reference>. The names of the twelve chiefs, <reference osisRef="Num.34.19-Num.34.29">Num 34:19-29</reference>.
entries.aaf07396ae5c15bec223661420c9ec335f10bfe4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen6286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6287" type="x-p"/> The land of Canaan with the coasts thereof - All description here is useless. The situation and boundaries of the land of Canaan can only be known by actual survey, or by consulting a good map.
entries.1fc190b5b19ca3aaca89e1fb2b0eee8fd8818607: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen6287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6288" type="x-p"/> The salt sea - The Dead Sea, or lake Asphaltites. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.19.25">Gen 19:25</reference>.
entries.eb0ff6000f7e73397f699743e951d8e1b60964c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen6288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6289" type="x-p"/> The river of Egypt - The eastern branch of the river Nile; or, according to others, a river which is south of the land of the Philistines, and fails into the gulf or bay near Calieh.
entries.ae525f4e6087043a9be0eba4754d61f7dd800fff: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen6289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6290" type="x-p"/> Ye shall even have the great sea for a border - The Mediterranean Sea, called here the Great Sea, to distinguish it from the Dead Sea, the Sea of Tiberias, etc., which were only a sort of lakes. In Hebrew there is properly but one term, ים yam, which is applied to all collections of water apparently stagnant, and which is generally translated sea. The Greek of the New Testament follows the Hebrew, and employs, in general, the word θαλασσα, Sea, whether it speaks of the Mediterranean, or of the sea or lake of Galilee.
entries.f34847e0e86941509a53135da6ebe3ff8bf78298: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen6290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6291" type="x-p"/> The sea of Chinnereth - The same as the sea of Galilee, sea of Tiberias, and sea of Gennesareth.
entries.e150790aef46959a7ecd62cbf4f662142cfb5eb6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen6291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6292" type="x-p"/> The border shall go down to Jordan - This river is famous both in the Old and New Testaments. It takes its rise at the foot of Mount Libanus, passes through the sea of Chinnereth or Tiberias, and empties itself into the lake Asphaltites or Dead Sea, from which it has no outlet. In and by it God wrought many miracles. God cut off the waters of this river as he did those of the Red Sea, so that they stood on a heap on each side, and the people passed over on dry ground. Both Elijah and Elisha separated its waters in a miraculous way, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.8-2Kgs.2.14">2Kgs 2:8-14</reference>. Naaman, the Syrian general, by washing in it at the command of the prophet, was miraculously cured of his leprosy, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.10-2Kgs.5.14">2Kgs 5:10-14</reference>. In this river John baptized great multitudes of Jews; and in it was Christ himself baptized, and the Spirit of God descended upon him, and the voice from heaven proclaimed him the great and only Teacher and Savior of men, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.16">Mat 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.17">Mat 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.1.5-Mar.1.11">Mar 1:5-11</reference>.
entries.7ea336eac346334319bf100aacb28df091144be0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen6292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6293" type="x-p"/> This is the land which ye shall inherit by lot - Much of what is said concerning this land is peculiarly emphatic. It is a land that contains a multitude of advantages in its climate, its soil, situation, etc. It is bounded on the south by a ridge of mountains, which separate it from Arabia, and screen it from the burning and often pestiferous winds which blow over the desert from that quarter. On the west it is bounded by the Mediterranean Sea; on the north, by Mount Libanus, which defends it from the cold northern blasts; and on the east by the river Jordan, and its fertile, well-watered plains. It is described by God himself as "a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains, and depths that spring out of valleys and hills; a land of wheat, and barley, and vines, and fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of olive oil and honey; a land wherein there was no scarcity of bread, and where both iron and copper mines abounded," <reference osisRef="Deu.8.7-Deu.8.9">Deu 8:7-9</reference> : a land finely diversified with hills and valleys, and well watered by the rain of heaven, in this respect widely different from Egypt; a land which God cared for, on which his eyes were continually placed from the beginning to the end of the year; watched over by a most merciful Providence; in a word, a land which flowed with milk and honey, and was the most pleasant of all lands; <reference osisRef="Deu.11.11">Deu 11:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.11.12">Deu 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference>. Such was the land, and such were the advantages that this most favored people were called to possess. They were called to possess it by lot that each might be satisfied with his possession, as considering it to be appointed to him by the especial providence of God; and its boundaries were ascertained on Divine authority, to prevent all covetousness after the territories of others.
entries.dee4b76ae98409d18b94e6d8cadd6ff81c0c4e7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen6293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6294" type="x-p"/> And the names of the men - are these - It is worthy of remark that Moses does not follow any order hitherto used of placing the tribes, neither that in Numbers 1, nor that in Numbers 7, nor that in Numbers 26, nor any other; but places them here exactly in that order in which they possessed the land. <div eID="gen6294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6295" type="x-p"/> 1. Benjamin <div eID="gen6297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6298" type="x-p"/> 4. Dan <div eID="gen6298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6299" type="x-p"/> 5. Zebulun <div eID="gen6301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6302" type="x-p"/> 8. Issachar <div eID="gen6302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6303" type="x-p"/> 9. Asher <div eID="gen6303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6304" type="x-p"/> 10. Naphtali <div eID="gen6304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6305" type="x-p"/> Judah is first, having the first lot; and he dwelt in the south part of the land, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.1">Jos 15:1</reference>, etc.; and next to him Simeon, because his inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.1">Jos 19:1</reference>. Benjamin was third; he had his inheritance by Judah, between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.11">Jos 18:11</reference>. Dan was the fourth; his lot fell westward of that of Benjamin, in the country of the Philistines, as may be seen in <reference osisRef="Jos.19.40">Jos 19:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.41">Jos 19:41</reference>, etc. Fifth, Manasseh; and sixth, by him, his brother Ephraim, whose inheritances were behind that of Benjamin, <reference osisRef="Jos.16.7">Jos 16:7</reference>. Next to these dwelt, seventh, Zebulun; and eighth, Issachar; concerning whose lots see <reference osisRef="Jos.19.10-Jos.19.17">Jos 19:10-17</reference>. Ninth, Asher; and tenth, Naphtali; see <reference osisRef="Jos.19.24">Jos 19:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.32">Jos 19:32</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen6305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6306" type="x-p"/> And as in encamping about the tabernacle they were arranged according to their fraternal relationship, (see Numbers 2)., so they were in the division and inheriting of the promised land. Judah and Simeon, both sons of Leah, dwelt abreast of each other. Benjamin, son of Rachel, and Dan, son of Rachel's maid, dwelt next abreast. Manasseh and Ephraim, both sons of Joseph, son of Rachel, had the next place abreast. Zebulun and Issachar, who dwelt next together, were both sons of Leah; and the last pair were Asher, of Leah's maid, and Naphtali, of Rachel's maid. Thus God, in nominating princes that should divide the land, signified beforehand the manner of their possession, and that they should be so situated as to dwell together as brethren in unity, for the mutual help and comfort of each other. See Ainsworth. In this arrangement there is much skill, judgment, and kindness every where displayed.  <chapter eID="Num.34"/> <div eID="gen6306" type="x-p"/>

entries.d27bdddd90fe9b2d1f12c585b055ad67a28046c5: Num 34:3-5 <div eID="gen2076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2077" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">southern boundary</hi> is the same as that given in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.2-Josh.15.4">Jos 15:2-4</reference> as the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Judah. We have first the general description, “<hi type="italic">The south side shall be to you from the desert of Zin on the sides of Edom onwards</hi>,” i.e., the land was to extend towards the south as far as the desert of Zin on the sides of Edom. על־ידי, “on the sides,” differs in this respect from על־יד, “on the side” (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.5">Exo 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.15.46">Jos 15:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.2">2Sa 15:2</reference>), that the latter is used to designate contact at a single point or along a short line; the former, contact for a long distance or throughout the whole extent (= כּל־יד, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.37">Deu 2:37</reference>). “<hi type="italic">On the sides of Edom</hi>” signifies, therefore, that the desert of Zin stretched along the side of Edom, and Canaan was separated from Edom by the desert of Zin. From this it follows still further, that Edom in this passage is not the mountains of Edom, which had their western boundary on the Arabah, but the country to the south of the desert of <hi type="italic">Zin</hi> or Wady <hi type="italic">Murreh</hi>, viz., the mountain land of the Azazimeh, which still bears the name of <hi type="italic">Seir</hi> or <hi type="italic">Serr</hi> among the Arabs (see <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rowland</hi> in <hi type="italic">Ritter's</hi> Erdk. xiv. pp. 840 and 1087). The statement in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.1">Jos 15:1</reference> also agrees with this, viz., that Judah’s inheritance was “to the territory of Edom, the desert of Zin towards the south,” according to which the desert of Zin was also to divide the territory of Edom from that of the tribe of Judah (see the remarks on Num 14:45). With <hi type="italic">Num 34:3</hi> the more minute description of the southern boundary line commences: “<hi type="italic">The south border shall be from the end of the Salt Sea eastward</hi>,” i.e., start from “the tongue which turns to the south” (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.2">Jos 15:2</reference>), from the southern point of the Dead Sea, where there is now a salt marsh with the salt mountain at the south-west border of the lake. “<hi type="italic">And turn to the south side</hi> (מנּגב) <hi type="italic">of the ascent of Akrabbim</hi>” (<hi type="italic">ascensus scorpionum</hi>), i.e., hardly “the steep pass of <hi type="italic">es Sufah</hi>, 1434 feet in height, which leads in a south-westerly direction from the Dead Sea along the northern side of Wady <hi type="italic">Fikreh</hi>, a wady three-quarters of an hour’s journey in breadth, and over which the road from Petra to Heshbon passes,”<note placement="foot">See Robinson, vol. ii. pp. 587, 591; and v. <hi type="italic">Schubert</hi>, ii. pp. 443, 447ff.</note> as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> maintains; for the expression נסב (turn), in Num 34:4, according to which the southern border turned at the height of Akrabbim, that is to say, did not go any farther in the direction from N.E. to S.W. than from the southern extremity of the Salt Sea to this point, and was then continued in a straight line from east to west, is not at all applicable to the position of this pass, since there would be no bend whatever in the boundary line at the pass of es Sufah, if it ran from the Arabah through Wady Fikreh, and so across to Kadesh. The “height of Akrabbim,” from which the country round was afterwards called Akrabattine, Akrabatene (1 Macc. 5:4; Josephus,<hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> 12:8, 1),<note placement="foot">It must be distinguished, however, from the <hi type="italic">Akrabatta</hi> mentioned by <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> in his Wars of the Jews (iii. 3, 5), the modern<hi type="italic">Akrabeh</hi> in central Palestine (<hi type="italic">Rob. Bibl. Res</hi>. p. 296), and from the toparchy <hi type="italic">Akrabattene</hi> mentioned in <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Wars of the Jews, ii. 12, 4; 20, 4; 22, 2), which was named after this place.</note> is most probably the lofty row of “white cliffs” of sixty or eighty feet in height, which run obliquely across the Arabah at a distance of about eight miles below the Dead Sea and, as seen from the south-west point of the Dead Sea, appear to shut in the Ghor, and which form the dividing line between the two sides of the great valley, which is called <hi type="italic">el Ghor</hi> on one side, and <hi type="italic">el Araba</hi> on the other (Robinson, ii. 489, 494, 502). Consequently it was not the Wady Fikreh, but a wady which opened into the Arabah somewhat farther to the south, possibly the southern branch of the Wady Murreh itself, which formed the actual boundary. <div eID="gen2077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2078" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And shall pass over to Zin</hi>” (i.e., the desert of Zin, the great Wady <hi type="italic">Murreh</hi>, see at Num 14:21), “<hi type="italic">and its going forth shall be to the south of Kadesh-barnea</hi>,” at the western extremity of the desert of Zin (see at Num 20:16). From this point the boundary went farther out (יצא) “<hi type="italic">to Hazar-Addar, and over</hi> (עבר) <hi type="italic">to Azmon</hi>.” According to <reference osisRef="Josh.15.3-Josh.15.4">Jos 15:3-4</reference>, it went to the south of Kadesh-barnea over (עבר) to Hezron, and ascended (עלה) to <hi type="italic">Addar</hi>, and then turned to <hi type="italic">Karkaa</hi>, and went over to <hi type="italic">Azmon</hi>. Consequently <hi type="italic">Hazar-Addar</hi> corresponds to <hi type="italic">Hezron</hi> and <hi type="italic">Addar</hi> (in Joshua); probably the two places were so close to each other that they could be joined together. Neither of them has been discovered yet. This also applies to Karkaa and Azmon. The latter name reminds us of the Bedouin tribe <hi type="italic">Azazimeh</hi>, inhabiting the mountains in the southern part of the desert of Zin (Robinson, i. pp. 274, 283, 287; <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, iii. pp. 45, 47). <hi type="italic">Azmon</hi> is probably to be sought for near the Wady <hi type="italic">el Ain</hi>, to the west of the Hebron road, and not far from its entrance into the Wady <hi type="italic">el Arish;</hi> for this is “<hi type="italic">the river</hi> (brook) <hi type="italic">of Egypt</hi>,” to which the boundary turned from Azmon, and through which it had “its outgoings at the sea,” i.e., terminated at the Mediterranean Sea. The “brook of Egypt,” therefore, is frequently spoken of as the southern boundary of the land of Israel (1Ki 8:65; 2Ki 24:7; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.8">2Ch 7:8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Isa 27:12</reference>, where the lxx express the name by Ῥινοκοροῦρα). Hence the southern boundary ran, throughout its whole length, from the Arabah on the east to the Mediterranean on the west, along valleys which form a natural division, and constitute more or less the boundary line between the desert and the cultivated land.<note placement="foot">On the lofty mountains of <hi type="italic">Madara</hi>, where the Wady <hi type="italic">Murreh</hi> is divided into two wadys (<hi type="italic">Fikreh</hi> and <hi type="italic">Murreh</hi>) which run to the Arabah,<hi type="italic">v. Schubert</hi> observed “some mimosen-trees,” with which, as he expresses it, “the vegetation of Arabia took leave of us, as it were, as they were the last that we saw on our road.” And <hi type="italic">Dieterici</hi> (<hi type="italic">Reisebilder</hi>, ii. pp. 156-7) describes the mountain ridge at <hi type="italic">Nakb es Sufah</hi> as “the boundary line between the yellow desert and green steppes,” and observes still further, that on the other side of the mountain (i.e., northwards) the plain spread out before him in its fresh green dress. “The desert journey was over, the empire of death now lay behind us, and a new life blew towards us from fields covered with green.” - In the same way the country between Kadesh and the Hebron road, which has become better known to us through the descriptions of travellers, is described as a natural boundary. <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, in his account of his journey from Hebron to Sinai (iii. p. 47), observes that the mountains of <hi type="italic">Tih</hi> commence at the <hi type="italic">Wady el Ain</hi> (fountain-valley), which takes its name from a fountain that waters thirty date-palms and a few small corn-fields (i.e., <hi type="italic">Ain el Kuderat</hi>, in Robinson, i. p. 280), and describes the country to the south of the small flat Wady <hi type="italic">el Kdeis</hi> (<hi type="italic">el Kideise</hi>), in which many tamarisks grew (i.e., no doubt a wady that comes from Kadesh, from which it derives its name), as a “most dreadful wilderness, which spreads out to an immeasurable extent in all directions, without trees, shrubs, or a single spot of green” (p. 50), although the next day he “found as an unexpected rarity another small field of barley, which might have been an acre in extent” (pp. 52, 53). Robinson (i. pp. 280ff.) also found, upon the route from Sinai to Hebron, more vegetation in the desert between the Wady <hi type="italic">el Kusaimeh</hi> and el Ain than anywhere else before throughout his entire journey; and after passing the Wady <hi type="italic">el Ain</hi> to the west of Kadesh, he “came upon a broad tract of tolerably fertile soil, capable of tillage, and apparently once tilled.” Across the whole of this tract of land there were long ranges of low stone walls visible (called “<hi type="italic">el Muzeiriât</hi>,” “little plantations,” by the Arabs), which had probably served at some former time as boundary walls between the cultivated fields. A little farther to the north the Wady <hi type="italic">es Serâm</hi> opens into an extended plain, which looked almost like a meadow with its bushes, grass, and small patches of wheat and barley. A few Azazimeh Arabs fed their camels and flocks here. The land all round became more open, and showed broad valleys that were capable of cultivation, and were separated by low and gradually sloping hills. The grass become more frequent in the valleys, and herbs were found upon the hills. “We heard (he says at p. 283) this morning for the first time the songs of many birds, and among them the lark.”</note>
entries.4c057bdbef6bddedfbcd6c744227b3012941b931: Num 34:6 <div eID="gen2078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2079" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">western boundary</hi> was to be “the great sea and its territory,” i.e., the Mediterranean Sea with its territory or coast (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.3.16-Deut.3.17">Deu 3:16-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.23">Jos 13:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.27">Jos 13:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.15.47">Jos 15:47</reference>).
entries.b446d65ebd9dee725f570b14dec21830648dd081: Num 34:7-9 <div eID="gen2079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2080" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">northern boundary</hi> cannot be determined with certainty. “<hi type="italic">From the great sea, mark out to you </hi>(תּתאוּ, from תּאה = תּוה, to mark or point out), i.e., fix, <hi type="italic">Mount Hor as the boundary</hi>” - from thence “<hi type="italic">to come to Hamath; and let the goings forth of the boundary be to Zedad. And the boundary shall go out to Ziphron, and its goings out be at Hazar-enan</hi>.” Of all these places, <hi type="italic">Hamath</hi>, the modern <hi type="italic">Hamah</hi>, or the <hi type="italic">Epiphania</hi> of the Greeks and Romans on the Orontes (see at Num 13:21, and <reference osisRef="Gen.10.18">Gen 10:18</reference>), is the only one whose situation is well known; but the geographical description of the northern boundary of the land of Israel חמת לבא (Num 13:21; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.5">Jos 13:5</reference>; Jdg 3:3; 1Ki 8:65; 2Ki 14:25; <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.5">1Ch 13:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.8">2Ch 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">Amo 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.15">Eze 47:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.20">Eze 47:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1">Eze 48:1</reference>) is so indefinite, that the boundary line cannot be determined with exactness. For no proof can be needed in the present day that חמת לבא cannot mean “to Hamath” (<hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> <hi type="italic">thes</hi>. i. p. 185; <hi type="italic">Studer</hi> on Jdg 3:3, and <hi type="italic">Baur</hi> on <reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">Amo 6:2</reference>), in such a sense as would make the town of Hamath the border town, and בּא a perfectly superfluous pleonasm. In all the passages mentioned, Hamath refers, not to the town of that name (<hi type="italic">Epiphania</hi> on the Orontes), but to the kingdom of Hamath, which was named after its capital, as is proved beyond all doubt by <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.4">2Ch 8:4</reference>, where Solomon is said to have built store cities “in Hamath.” The city of Hamath never belonged to the kingdom of Israel, not even under David and Solomon, and was not reconquered by Jeroboam II, as Baur supposes (see my Commentary on the Books of Kings, and <hi type="italic">Thenius</hi> on 2Ki 14:25). How far the territory of the kingdom of Hamath extended towards the south in the time of Moses, and how much of it was conquered by Solomon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.4">2Ch 8:4</reference>), we are nowhere informed. We simply learn from 2Ki 25:21, that Riblah (whether the same Riblah as is mentioned in Num 34:11 as a town upon the eastern boundary, is very doubtful) was situated in the land of Hamath in the time of the Chaldeans. Now if this Riblah has been preserved in the modern <hi type="italic">Ribleh</hi>, a miserable village on the Orontes, in the northern part of the <hi type="italic">Bekaa</hi>, ten or twelve hours’ journey to the south-west of <hi type="italic">Hums</hi>, and fourteen hours to the north of <hi type="italic">Baalbek</hi> (Robinson, iii. p. 461, App. 176, and Bibl. Researches, p. 544), the land of Canaan would have reached a little farther northwards, and almost to <hi type="italic">Hums</hi> (<hi type="italic">Emesa</hi>). <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> moves the boundary still farther to the north. He supposes Mount <hi type="italic">Hor</hi> to be <hi type="italic">Mons Casius</hi>, to the south-west of Antioch, on the Orontes, and agrees with Robinson (iii. 461) in identifying <hi type="italic">Zedad</hi>, in the large village of <hi type="italic">Zadad</hi> (<hi type="italic">Sudud</hi> in <hi type="italic">Rob</hi>.), which is inhabited exclusively by Syriac Christians, who still speak Syriac according to <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi> (i. 32 and 279), a town containing about 3000 inhabitants (<hi type="italic">Wetstein</hi>, <hi type="italic">Reiseber</hi>. p. 88), to the south-east of <hi type="italic">Hums</hi>, on the east of the road from Damascus to Hunes, a short day’s journey to the north of <hi type="italic">Nebk</hi>, and four (or, according to <hi type="italic">Van de Velde's</hi> memoir, from ten to twelve) hours’ journey to the south of <hi type="italic">Hasya</hi> (Robinson, iii. p. 461; Ritter, Erdk. xvii. pp. 1443-4).<hi type="italic">Ziphron</hi>, which was situated upon the border of the territory of Hamath and Damascus, if it is the same as the one mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.16">Eze 47:16</reference>, is supposed by <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> and <hi type="italic">Wetstein</hi> (p. 88) to be preserved in the ruins of Zifran, which in all probability have never been visited by any European, fourteen hours to the north-east of Damascus, near to the road from Palmyra. Lastly, Hazar-enan (equivalent to fountain-court) is supposed to be the station called <hi type="italic">Centum Putea</hi> (Πούτεα in <hi type="italic">Ptol</hi>. v. 15, 24), mentioned in the <hi type="italic">Tabul</hi>. <hi type="italic">Peuting</hi>. x. 3, on the road from <hi type="italic">Apamia</hi> to <hi type="italic">Palmyra</hi>, twenty-seven miles, or about eleven hours, to the north-west of Palmyra. - But we may say with certainty that all these conclusions are incorrect, because they are irreconcilable with the eastern boundary described in Num 34:10, Num 34:11. For example, according to Num 34:10, Num 34:11, the Israelites were to draw (fix) the eastern boundary “from <hi type="italic">Hazar-enan</hi> to <hi type="italic">Shepham</hi>,” which, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> observes, “cannot be determined with exactness, but was farther south than <hi type="italic">Hazar-enan</hi>, as it was a point on the eastern boundary which is traced here from north to south, and also farther west, as we may infer from the allusion to Riblah, probably at the northern end of Antilibanus”. From <hi type="italic">Shepham</hi> the boundary was “<hi type="italic">to go down to Riblah</hi>,” which <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> finds in the <hi type="italic">Ribleh</hi> mentioned above. Now, if we endeavour to fix the situation of these places according to the latest and most trustworthy maps, the incorrectness of the conclusions referred to becomes at once apparent. From <hi type="italic">Zadad</hi> (<hi type="italic">Sudad</hi>) to <hi type="italic">Zifran</hi>, the line of the northern boundary would not have gone from west to east, but from north to south, or rather towards the south-west, and from <hi type="italic">Zifran</hi> to <hi type="italic">Centum Putea</hi> still more decidedly in a south-westerly direction. Consequently the northern boundary would have described a complete semicircle, commencing in the north-west and terminating in the south-east. But if even in itself this appears very incredible, it becomes perfectly impossible when we take the eastern boundary into consideration. For if this went down to the south-west from <hi type="italic">Hazar-enan</hi> to <hi type="italic">Shepham</hi> according to <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> conclusions, instead of going down (Num 34:11) from <hi type="italic">Shepham</hi> to <hi type="italic">Riblah</hi>, it would have gone up six or seven geographical miles from south to north, and then have gone down again from north to south along the eastern coast of the Lake of Gennesareth. Now it is impossible that Moses should have fixed such a boundary to the land of Israel on the north-east, and equally impossible that a later Hebrew, acquainted with the geography of his country, should have described it in this way. <div eID="gen2080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2081" type="x-p"/> If, in order to obtain a more accurate view of the extent of the land towards the north and north-east, we compare the statements of the book of Joshua concerning the conquered land with the districts which still remained to be taken at the time of the distribution; Joshua had taken the land “from the bald mountain which ascends towards Seir,” i.e., probably the northern ridge of the <hi type="italic">Azazimeh</hi> mountains, with its white masses of chalk (<hi type="italic">Fries, ut sup</hi>. p. 76; see also at <reference osisRef="Josh.11.17">Jos 11:17</reference>), “to <hi type="italic">Baal-Gad</hi>, in the valley of Lebanon, below Mount <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.17">Jos 11:17</reference>; cf. Num 12:7). But <hi type="italic">Baal-Gad</hi> in the valley (בּקעה) of Lebanon is not <hi type="italic">Heliopolis</hi> (now <hi type="italic">Baalbek</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Bekaa</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Coelesyria</hi>), as many, from <hi type="italic">Iken</hi> and <hi type="italic">J. D. Michaelis</hi> down to <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, suppose; for “the <hi type="italic">Bekaa</hi> is not under the <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi>,” and “there is no proof, or even probability, that Joshua’s conquests reached so far, or that Baalbek was ever regarded as the northern boundary of Palestine, nor even that the adjoining portion of Anti-Lebanon was ever called Hermon” (Robinson, <hi type="italic">Biblical Researches</hi>, p. 409). <hi type="italic">Baal-Gad</hi>, which is called <hi type="italic">Baal-Hermon</hi> in Jdg 3:3 and <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.23">1Ch 5:23</reference>, was the later <hi type="italic">Paneas</hi> or <hi type="italic">Caesarea Philippi</hi>, the modern <hi type="italic">Banias</hi>, at the foot of the Hermon (cf. <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> p. 245; Rob. Bibl. Res. pp. 408-9, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> iii. pp. 347ff.). This is placed beyond all doubt by <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.23">1Ch 5:23</reference>, according to which the Manassites, who were increasing in numbers, dwelt “from Bashan to Baal-hermon, and Senir, and the mountains of Hermon,” since this statement proves that Baal-hermon was between Bashan and the mountains of Hermon. In harmony with this, the following places in the north of Canaan are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.4-Josh.13.5">Jos 13:4-5</reference>, and Jdg 3:3, as being left unconquered by Joshua: - (1.) “All the land of the Canaanites (i.e., of the Phoenicians who dwelt on the coast), and the cave of the Sidonians to Aphek;” מערה, probably the <hi type="italic">spelunca inexpugnabilis in territorio Sidoniensi, quae vulgo dicitur cavea de Tyrum</hi> (<hi type="italic">Wilh. Tyr</hi>. xix. 11), the present <hi type="italic">Mughr Jezzin</hi>, i.e., caves of <hi type="italic">Jezzin</hi>, to the east of Sidon upon Lebanon (<hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, <hi type="italic">Erdk</hi>. xvii. pp. 99, 100); and <hi type="italic">Aphek</hi>, probably the modern <hi type="italic">Afka</hi>, to the north-east of Beirut (Robinson, Bibl. Res.). (2.) “The land of the <hi type="italic">Giblites</hi>,” i.e., the territory of Byblos, and “all Lebanon towards the east, from Baal-Gad below Hermon, till you come to Hamath,” i.e., not Antilibanus, but Lebanon, which lies to the east of the land of the Giblites. The land of the Giblites, or territory of <hi type="italic">Gebal</hi>, which is cited here as the northernmost district of the unconquered land, so that its northern boundary must have coincided with the northern boundary of Canaan, can hardly have extended to the latitude of Tripoli, but probably only reached to the cedar grove at <hi type="italic">Bjerreh</hi>, in the neighbourhood of which the highest peaks of the Lebanon are found. The territory of the tribes of Asher and Naphtali (Josh 19:24-39) did not reach farther up than this. From all these accounts, we must not push the northern boundary of Canaan as far as the <hi type="italic">Eleutherus</hi>, <hi type="italic">Nahr el Kebir</hi>, but must draw it farther to the south, across the northern portion of the Lebanon; so that we may look for <hi type="italic">Hazar-enan</hi> (fountain-court), which is mentioned as the end of the northern boundary, and the starting-point of the eastern, near the fountain of <hi type="italic">Lebweh</hi>. This fountain forms the water-shed in the Bekaa, between the Orontes, which flows to the north, and the Leontes, which flows to the south (cf. Robinson, Bibl. Res. p. 531), and is not only a very large fountain of the finest clear water, springing at different points from underneath a broad piece of coarse gravel, which lies to the west of a vein of limestone, but the whole of the soil is of such a character, that “you have only to dig in the gravel, to get as many springs as you please.” The quantity of water which is found here is probably even greater than that at the <hi type="italic">Anjar</hi>. In addition to the four principal streams, there are three or four smaller ones (Robinson, Bibl. Res. p. 532), so that this place might be called, with perfect justice, by the name of <hi type="italic">fountain-court</hi>. The probability of this conjecture is also considerably increased by the fact, that the <hi type="italic">Ain</hi>, mentioned in Num 34:11 as a point upon the eastern boundary, can also be identified without any difficulty (see at Num 34:11).
entries.e3de0c1dd0db433db124af4eecdc41d40343384a: Num 34:10-12 <div eID="gen2081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2082" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Eastern Boundary</hi>. - If we endeavour to trace the upper line of the eastern boundary from the fountain-place just mentioned, it ran from <hi type="italic">Hazar-enan</hi> to <hi type="italic">Shepham</hi>, the site of which is unknown, and “from <hi type="italic">Shepham</hi> it was to go down to <hi type="italic">Riblah</hi>, on the east of <hi type="italic">Ain</hi>” (the fountain). The article הרבלה, and still more the precise description, “to the east of Ain, the fountain, or fountain locality” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>), show plainly that this <hi type="italic">Riblah</hi> is to be distinguished from the <hi type="italic">Riblah</hi> in the land of Hamath (2Ki 23:33; 2Ki 25:21; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.27">Jer 52:27</reference>), with which it is mostly identified. <hi type="italic">Ain</hi> is supposed to be “the great fountain of <hi type="italic">Neba Anjar</hi>, at the foot of Antilibanus, which is often called <hi type="italic">Birket Anjar</hi>, on account of its taking its rise in a small reservoir or pool” (Robinson, Bibl. Res. p. 498), and near to which <hi type="italic">Mej-del-Anjar</hi> is to be seen, consisting of “the ruins of the walls and towers of a fortified town, or rather of a large citadel” (Robinson, p. 496; cf. Ritter, xvii. pp. 181ff.).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> regards <hi type="italic">Ain</hi> as the source of the Orontes, i.e., <hi type="italic">Neba Lebweh</hi>, and yet, notwithstanding this, identifies <hi type="italic">Riblah</hi> with the village of <hi type="italic">Ribleh</hi> mentioned above. But can this <hi type="italic">Ribleh</hi>, which is at least eight hours to the north of <hi type="italic">Neba Lebweh</hi>, be described as on the east of <hi type="italic">Ain</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Neba Lebweh?</hi></note> <div eID="gen2082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2083" type="x-p"/> From this point the boundary went farther down, and pressed (מחה) “upon the shoulder of the lake of <hi type="italic">Chinnereth</hi> towards the east,” i.e., upon the north-east shore of the Sea of Galilee (see <reference osisRef="Josh.19.35">Jos 19:35</reference>). Hence it ran down along the Jordan to the Salt Sea (Dead Sea). According to these statements, therefore, the eastern boundary went from Bekaa along the western slopes of Antilibanus, over or past <hi type="italic">Rasbeya</hi> and <hi type="italic">Banyas</hi>, at the foot of Hermon, along the edge of the mountains which bound the <hi type="italic">Huleh</hi> basin towards the east, down to the north-east corner of the Sea of Galilee; so that <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi> itself (<hi type="italic">Jebel es Sheikh</hi>) did not belong to the land of Israel.
entries.089da7b90afa120399be995326f25dc7ab076684: Num 34:13-15 <div eID="gen2083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2084" type="x-p"/> This land, according to the boundaries thus described, the Israelites were to distribute by lot (Num 26:56), to give it to the nine tribes and a half, as the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh had already received their inheritance on the other side of the Jordan (Num 32:33.).
entries.1c760af7525291a7de18e4406e2d3aec7791c3f3: Num 34:16-29 <div eID="gen2084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2085" type="x-p"/> List of the Men Appointed to Distribute the Land. - In addition to Eleazar and Joshua, the former of whom was to stand at the head as high priest, in accordance with the divine appointment in Num 27:21, and the latter to occupy the second place as commander of the army, a prince was selected from each of the ten tribes who were interested in the distribution, as Reuben and Gad had nothing to do with it. Of these princes, namely heads of fathers’ houses of the tribes (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.1">Jos 14:1</reference>), not heads of tribes (see at Num 13:2), Caleb, who is well known from Num 13, is the only one whose name if known. The others are not mentioned anywhere else. The list of tribes, in the enumeration of their princes, corresponds, with some exceptions, to the situation of the territory which the tribes received in Canaan, reckoning from south to north, and deviates considerably from the order in which the lots came out for the different tribes, as described in Josh 15-19. נחל in the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, in Num 34:17 and Num 34:18, signifies to give for an inheritance, just as in <reference osisRef="Exod.34.8">Exo 34:8</reference>, to put into possession. There is not sufficient ground for altering the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> into <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, especially as the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> in Num 34:29 is construed with the accusative of the person, and with the thing governed by ב; whereas in Num 34:17 the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> is construed with the person governed by ל, and the accusative of the thing.  <chapter eID="Num.34"/> <div eID="gen2085" type="x-p"/>

entries.907a9398bd69259f2389163be802d9ff7b388f3b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.34.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.34.1" sID="gen21627" type="section"/> <div sID="gen21628" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the Lord spake unto Moses.</hi> God here undertakes the office of a prudent and careful father of a family, in fixing the boundaries of the land on every side, lest their right to posses it should ever be called in question. He begins on the southern side, where it must be observed that the district of Bashan is included in it, and all that the Israelites had acquired before their passage of the Jordan, so that this addition was approved of by God. He extends this part as far as the wilderness of Sin, and the borders of Edom, and brings it round from Kadesh-barnea to Addar, and the passage of Azmon, and, finally, to the stream which washes <note n="228"> <div sID="gen21629" type="x-p"/> There has been much discussion amongst the commentators on this point. The conclusion to which Dr. Kitto comes, after due examination of the opposite theory, is, that “the river of Egypt,” when mentioned as a boundary, cannot mean the Nile. “The present ‘river of Egypt’ (he adds) probably denotes a stream which formed the extreme boundary of the country eastward of the Nile, which Egypt, even in these early times, professed to claim, and which derived its name from that circumstance. It was probably not far from El-Arish, to which, under the name of Rhinocorura, it is expressly referred by the Septuagint. That it was a stream somewhere between the southern frontier of Palestine and the Nile we are deeply convinced.” — Illustr. Com., <hi type="italic">in</hi> <hi type="italic">loco.</hi><div eID="gen21629" type="x-p"/> </note> the city of Rhinocorura, in the immediate vicinity of Egypt; for by “the river of Egypt” the Nile is by no means to be understood, the course of which was not at all in that direction. The southern boundary, therefore, was from the Mediterranean Sea towards Arabia. On the western side the land was washed by the Mediterranean Sea, which is here called “the Great Sea,” in comparison with the Lake of Gennesareth, and the Salt Sea, by which name the <hi type="italic">Lacus Asphaltires </hi>is here meant. The beginning of the northern boundary was the promontory of Hor, for it would not accord to suppose that the mountain is here referred to in which Aaron died, and which was far away, and situated on the opposite side of the land. It extended from hence to Epiphania in Syria, which is called Hamath; for I agree with Jerome in thinking that there were two cities of this name, and it is undoubtedly probable that Antioch is called “Hamath the great” by the Prophet Amos (<reference osisRef="Bible:Amos.6.2">Amos 6:2</reference>,) in comparison with the lesser city here mentioned, the name of which was given it by that wicked and cruel tyrant (Antiochus) Epiphanes; whether, however, the greater Antioch was formerly called Hamath and Riblab, as Jerome states, I leave undecided. It then passed on to Zedad and Ziphron, and its extremity was the village of Enan. The eastern boundary passed from thence through Shephan, Riblah, and Ain, until it reached the Lake of Gennesareth, a lake sufficiently well known, and here called the Sea of Chinnereth. Thus the eastern boundary pointed from Arabia in the direction of Persia, and Babylon was situated to the north-east of it.<div eID="gen21628" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.34.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen21627" osisID="Num.34.1" type="section"/>
entries.fd4222e29c54876b34759effce0a074bbe0aa120: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.34.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.34.13" sID="gen21630" type="section"/> <div sID="gen21631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">And Moses commanded the children of Israel.</hi> Though this is a repetition, yet it is not a superfluous one; for he contrasts the new allotment of the nine tribes and a half with the former grant; <note n="229"> <div sID="gen21632" type="x-p"/> “La donation qui avoit este desia faite de la region de Basan;” the grant which had been already made of the district of Bashan. — <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen21632" type="x-p"/> </note> for the exception, which is immediately added, as to the lands beyond Jordan, given to the Reubenites, and Gadites, and half tribe of Manasseh, does not exclude them from their part of the promised inheritance was if they were disinherited, and therefore banished beyond the boundaries prescribed by God — but only from being subject to the casting of lots, because they had by special privilege obtained from their brethren what would else have been included in the common inheritance. Not that this had been revealed from the beginning, but because God in His indulgence had complied with their request, whereby they enlarged the boundaries of the land. And assuredly it would have been absurd that no place should be given them among their brethren in the promised land, as if they were cast off from the family of Abraham. We have lately seen that this part, which seemed to be separated from the others, was included in the limits laid down by God. Moses, therefore, merely wished to declare that what remained was to be divided by lot.<div eID="gen21631" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.34.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen21630" osisID="Num.34.13" type="section"/>

16 And the Lord spake unto Moses. The question here arises, if the Israelites were to divide the land among themselves by lot, wherefore was the authority of the judges required, as if there was anything for them to decide? But if we consider what has been lately shown, that reference was to be had, in the distribution of the land, to the numbers in every tribe, it was requisite for two purposes, — first, that God might show by His decree the districts respectively assigned to them; and, secondly, that their dimensions might be proportionate to the number of their occupants. For the casting of lots was still necessary, because many would have been averse to the sea-coast, or would have preferred the center of the land to its extremities, or would have been unwilling to be banished to the mountains; in short, they would have contended with each other beyond measure in murmurings and strife. On this account the lots were cast, by the decision of which God placed the several tribes in whatever position He pleased, although the judges, together with the High Priest and Joshua, had before divided the land into ten portions. But after it was declared in what district the several tribes were to dwell, as if God had there designated their abodes, the determination of men was again necessarily had recourse to, as to how far, and in what direction, the boundaries of the greater tribes were to extend; otherwise the lesser tribes would have refused to be cooped up in a less convenient position. And although the supreme authority was justly vested in Eleazar and Joshua, lest God should expose them to calumny and ill-will, He associated with them a council, in which also there was a prudent precaution against rivalry, for each of the twelve tribes contributed its judge to preside over the distribution, so that none might complain of being aggrieved. Moreover, inasmuch as it was of great importance that the possession, once established, should be secured to posterity, first of all the names of the princes are recorded, in order to give certainty to the history; and, secondly, as had been stated at the beginning of the chapter, so also it is repeated at the end that they were chosen by God, from whence the Israelites learnt that the boundaries then fixed could not be altered without overthrowing the authority of God Himself.

                  <ns0:p n="17">17 These <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the names of the men which shall divide the land unto you: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 14. 1. and 19. 51.</ns0:note> Eleazar the priest <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Who was to act in Gods name, to cast lots, to prevent dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferences and contentions, to consult with God in cases of diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culty, to transact the whole business in a solemn and religious manner.</ns0:note>, and Joshua the son of Nun.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And ye shall take one prince of every tribe, to divide the land by inheritance.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And the names of the men <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> these: of the tribe of Judah <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The order of the Tribes is here differing from that <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 1, 7, 26. and in other places, being here, as also <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 16. and 17. and 18. and 19. conformed to the order of their several inheritances which afterwards fell to them by Lot. Which is an evident demonstration of the infinite wisdom of Gods pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vidence and of his exact and peculiar care over his people.</ns0:note>, Caleb the son of Jephun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neh.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And of the tribe of the children of Simeon, Shemuel the son of Ammihud.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chisbon.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And the prince of the tribe of the children of Dan, Bukki the son of Jogli.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 The prince of the children of Joseph: for the tribe of the children of Manasseh, Hanniel the son of Ephod.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And the prince of the tribe of the children of Ephraim, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And the prince of the tribe of the children of Zebulun, Elizaphan the son of Parnach.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And the prince of the tribe of the children of Issachar, Paltiel the son of Azzan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And the prince of the tribe of the children of Asher, Ahihud the son of Shelomi.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And the prince of the tribe of the children of Naphtali; Pedahel the son of Ammihud.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 These <ns0:hi>are they</ns0:hi> whom the LORD command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to divide the inheritance unto the children of Israel, in the land of Canaan.</ns0:p>
